title: Precepts 3
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer reads a 1995 talk by Sojun Weitsman from a Berkeley Zen Center newsletter, which fits the retreat's theme of taking refuge in the Triple Treasure. Before reading, Norman describes Mel as a plain priest met while raking leaves, who gave Norman a spare room in a hard season and shared quiet lunches under a plum tree. The reading names the teacher as one leg beside Dharma and Sangha, urges seeing a teacher's faults along with abilities, and ends with Joshu's willingness to listen to a seven-year-old girl. Norman then returns to the bodhisattva precepts, covering the three pure precepts and the ten grave precepts in brief. The closing instruction is to sit easily and let the body melt into the cushion.

sentences.text: Well, while I was getting myself ready to come to this retreat, I knew I was going to be gone for just about a week, so I opened up my mail, which had been piling up just in case of disaster.

I was whipping through all this mail, and among many other newsletters from different Buddhist groups I found a newsletter from the Berkeley Zen Center that had in it a talk by my teacher, Sojun Weitsman.
Even though I was just glancing at it, it seemed so wonderful that I threw it in my briefcase and brought it with me.
Since this talk, which is brief in the newsletter, is apropos of what I was speaking of yesterday, taking refuge in the Triple Treasure, I thought I would just read you the talk today.
It was so wonderful to me that I wanted to share it with you.
It seemed somehow relevant.
Those of you who know me well and have attended many retreats and talks of mine know that I almost never mention my teacher.
You'd think that I never had any teachers.
I don't know why I don't speak of him, because I actually think of him quite often.
But nowadays I don't see him very much.
Maybe three or four times a year I notice that it's been a while since I've seen him, so I call him up and visit.
So I don't know why I don't ever mention him.
Maybe it's because there isn't that much to say about him.
He's a very plain and ordinary person, really.
He's not famous or controversial or all that interesting.
I remember when I first met him, I looked up the Berkeley Zen Center in the phone book, and I went there and he was raking leaves out in front of the building.
I thought he was the gardener.
I said to him, "Who's the Roshi here?"
And he said, "There is no Roshi, just a priest."
Only later I realized that it was him who was the priest.
He didn't say, "I'm the priest," he said, "There's just a priest."
When I was thinking about that this morning, I realized that probably that's the reason why I really don't like the term Roshi, and I don't myself use the term.
People don't notice particularly that I don't use it, but I don't.
Because I don't consider myself a Roshi, I'm just a priest.
There have been meetings of Western Dharma teachers to consider the use of things like the term Roshi.
It turns out that I'm qualified, I want you to know, because there's actually a list of qualifications.
According to the American Soto Zen establishment, here are the qualifications.
You have to be over 50 years old, so I got that down.
You have to have received Dharma transmission and been a fully ordained priest for 10 years, so I have that.
You also have to have ordained students and trained students as head monk, which I've also done.
So I could be a Roshi, but I'm not.
I'm just a priest.
The funny thing about all this is that now my teacher uses the term Roshi.
So he finally got to be a Roshi.
But I figure there's plenty of Roshis out there.
Too many, I think.
We don't need another one.
So anyway, even though he is called Roshi, I actually don't call him Roshi.
I don't even call him my teacher.
I never even particularly think of him that way.
I call him Mel, which is his name.
It's the name his parents gave him.
When I went to look for him, I wasn't looking for a teacher.
I was looking to practice on my own.
I never could see the point of having a teacher.
As my father told me from the time I was about 12 until the day he died, "You're too stubborn to learn anything from anyone."
Which I think is actually true.
So my teacher didn't really teach me anything.
He just practiced with me side by side for a number of years, and for a while we lived together in the Berkeley Zen Center.
I was young in those days and I had a lot of suffering in my life.
I remember one time when I was in deep waters of suffering.
I didn't really have any place to live or any job or anything like that.
It was not a very good period in my life.
And he took me in.
He let me live in his house.
There was an extra room, and he put me in the room there.
He didn't bother me.
He didn't console me.
He didn't talk to me.
He just gave me the room.
I would read and write a lot and sit in my room alone.
Then we sat together every day, and that was it.
He didn't in those days even conduct dokusan, so we hardly ever had any kind of conversations.
The only time we ever really talked much was once in a while when we would have lunch together under an old plum tree.
He had a big garden in the back there.
He loved the garden.
He had a big plum tree there, and we would sit under the plum tree and have lunch.
I can remember the plum blossoms falling.
A little breeze comes and the plum blossoms fall down like snow.
I remember the lunch.
We usually had a little bit of thin, what do you call it, rye bread or something like that with some nice cheese and really good green tea.
But even then we hardly said much.
We would sit there and eat quietly.
So it's really true: he never taught me anything.
Which I think was exactly what I needed.
Whenever I say anything about him, I always say he never taught me anything.
He would hear about this, and I think it made him a little mad.
A few years ago he gave me a rakisu.
On the back of it he wrote, "I have nothing to give you but my Zen spirit."
And I think that's true.
I did receive from him his Zen spirit.
His Zen spirit is just the spirit of everyday Zen.
Just regular, ordinary, American life, Zen practice.
That's the life that he always lived.
He is, I think, most admirable to me for his strong common sense, faith and stability and steadfastness just to do the practice, no matter what.
After those early years practicing with Mel, I went to Tassajara Monastery.
I just left him in the Berkeley Zen Center, as many students did in those days.
I didn't realize that teachers are actually regular people, that they have feelings and so on, and that maybe it would matter to him that I would just up and leave for good and never come back.
That never occurred to me.
I don't think I ever said goodbye or thanks or anything.
I just sort of left, and that was that.
I was so self-centered, I think, that it never occurred to me that it might matter to him.
Or somehow I had this idea that teachers were beyond human feeling.
Later, though, maybe about 20 years later, I did recognize what had happened there, and I had a chance to apologize.
He never minded, really.
Actually, he felt it, but it wasn't something that bothered him.
So when I apologized to him, it wasn't a big deal to him.
But I was able to apologize to him and thank him for all that he had done for me by not doing anything.
In fact, in recent years, when we get together, we just talk very familiarly.
No big deal.
We have lunch together and we talk about our lives.
It's wonderful when we see each other, because he's really like my family, more than anything.
Like my closest family.
He's known me for more than 30 years, and we've been connected heart to heart for over 30 years.
So anyway, I did go to Tassajara and left all that behind.

I studied for about a dozen years with Baker Roshi, who ordained me, despite my many misgivings, not only about being a priest, but especially about living at Zen Center, about which I had many misgivings and dissatisfactions for 25 years.
But now I'm free of all of that.
I also studied significantly with a number of other teachers.
But in the end, after all that, I did come back to my original teacher and received Dharma transmission from him.
So this is all the introduction.
I haven't spoken about him, and most of you don't know much about him, so I thought I would say that little bit about him as an introduction to this wonderful talk.
You'll hear, I think, in this talk, all these qualities that I'm speaking of: just solid, ordinary, common sense, everyday Zen.
This lecture was given January 30, 1995.
I don't know where; it doesn't say where.
*The practice of teacher and student must be built on trust.
But the main thing is that the student should be able to trust himself or herself.
The purpose of having a teacher is to help the student become self-reliant.
I remember Suzuki Roshi saying, when the student comes, the teacher should turn the student out.
In other words, you don't bring the student in and make some kind of home for her.
The student must find her own way.
But a good teacher also matures the student.
It depends on the circumstances.
It's like dealing with a child.*
*You nurture the child, but you also let the child be a little stretched.
The child is out there on the edge, reaching for how to stand up, reaching for how to walk, how to climb, how to take care of himself.
The teacher's aim is to help the student stand up on their own.
Sometimes the student has to lean on the teacher, which is okay, but only for a while.
Like with children, a mother goes to the playground with her child, and the child goes off to play with the other kids.
At some point, the child remembers, hey, where's my mom?
The child goes back to check in with mom.
Oh, everything's fine.
And then the child goes out and plays again.
The child is always checking in.
Oh, yeah, where's my mom?*
*It's sometimes like that with a student and teacher.
My relationship with Suzuki Roshi was like that.
I would check in with him.
I would bring him a problem.
We would sit down and look at the problem.
Then he would turn it into a koan for me.
Not by saying, this is your koan, but making me think about it in a different way.
And then he would say to me, I'm sorry, you came to me with a problem, and I've given you another problem.
And we would laugh.
I'd go away and practice with my koan, and then I'd come back.
Back and forth.
I had to work hard on my own.
This coming and going was the way of developing my practice and my relationship with him.
Sometimes I did practice very close with him.
Sometimes we worked together for a period of time.*
*The whole point was to enable me to know how to have my own practice and gain my own self-reliance.
Even if something happened to my teacher, I would be able to stand on my own.
Some students rely heavily on the teacher.
They don't rely so much on the Dharma, and they don't rely so much on the Sangha.
Some people rely a lot on the Dharma, but they don't rely so much on the teacher, and they don't rely so much on the Sangha.
Some people are very social, and they rely a lot on the Sangha, but they don't care much for the Dharma.
And as for the teacher, it's okay that he's there.
So you have these three types.
A well-rounded student includes all three.*
*So a teacher is one leg.
If suddenly your teacher turns out to be a false teacher in some way, even though you may be crushed, you still have your own practice, which is practice of the Dharma and practice with the Sangha.
You can always find another teacher.
Or you can practice on your own until you find another teacher.
So you're not completely thrown.
But if you rely only on a teacher when the teacher is no longer there, you have nothing.
You can always take refuge in the Sangha when there is no teacher.
You can always study and take refuge in the Dharma when there is no teacher.*
*According to legend, when Shakyamuni Buddha was dying, Ananda asked him, Who is going to take your place?
And Shakyamuni said, The Dharma and the Sangha will take my place.
Just follow the path with diligence.
Teachers appear, and they're important.
They are a focal point and more.
But no matter who the teacher is, he is still a student.
There's a place called the place beyond learning.
But nobody has arrived there yet.
So don't worry about it.
If your teacher says, I have come to the place beyond learning, you should probably find another teacher.*
*It's important to be able to see the teacher's faults as well as the teacher's ability.
And if you feel that the teacher has ability, then you can weigh whether or not you can practice with that teacher and not ignore his faults.
But your eyes should always be open, and you should always know the difference between the teacher's abilities and the teacher's faults or problems.
Because the teacher, whoever that person is, has both.*
*Like in choosing a mate, we say, love is blind.
You see these wonderful qualities that you like about this person.
At the same time, you know that there are other qualities that you are not sure about.
But because the qualities you like tend to ignore the others, later on, these other problems that make you uncomfortable begin to emerge.
So you have to have your eyes open to both sides.
And when you get together with someone, it's important to reflect, well, what are the faults of this person that I'm going to have to deal with?
When we accept something good, the other side is already there.
Happiness and suffering, they go together.
So what kind of discomfort am I willing to accept?*
*With your teacher, it's the same.
So you should know, these are the teacher's faults.
They're not his attributes.
We tend to trust someone when they easily acknowledge their faults.
If you know your teacher thoroughly, you should know what to accept and how to help him or her.
It's not just one way*
that the teacher is helping the student.
The student is also helping the teacher.
When the relationship is there, it goes both ways.
Sometimes the student is the teacher and the teacher is the student.
If the teacher never allows the student to be the teacher, that's a dominating role.
Some people like taking a dominating role and some people like to be dominated.
And some people like to be treated like children.
But if the teacher keeps the student always in an adolescent role, then she is not really doing the student a favor.

If you feel that your teacher is keeping you in an adolescent role, you should question that, because the teacher should keep moving toward maturing the student, helping the student to become an adult.
Uchiyama Roshi says, the meaning of bodhisattva is adult.
The teacher would like the students to be bodhisattvas, adults, acting in responsible ways, truly grown up.
Sometimes the teacher is not completely grown up himself.
And the students have to help the teacher to grow.
It goes both ways.
However, even when the roles are reversed, the teacher is the teacher and the student is the student.
They are not peers.
If you are the abbot, which he is, the abbot of the Berkeley Zen Center, which he has been for many years, you have to be able to listen to the newest student.
Sometimes when you have a monastic situation and a staff of experienced people, the staff tends to be a closed circle.
They just listen to each other while there is this whole group of people who are not being heard or acknowledged.
So it's important to help hear everyone, to listen to everyone.
Sometimes the newest student can see something which everyone else misses.
When Joshu went out at 80 years old on pilgrimage and she said, "Even if I meet a little girl of seven years old who knows the Dharma better than I do, I'll listen to her."
And that's the end of the talk.
Isn't that wonderful?
I think it's just what I would say.
So I didn't want to read that talk and say all this, because we don't have time for it.
But I couldn't resist, and I thought to myself, well, I'll save this for another time later, but surely I would forget.
I thought I would share that with you this morning.
However, now we must get back to the main job: 13 precepts.
So I was thinking that what we should do is extend the retreat by two or three days.
Is everybody okay with that?
I'm just kidding.
Don't worry.
So here we go. 13 bodhisattva precepts.
So we did the first three.
I take refuge in Buddha, Dharma, Sangha.
Now we have the next three bodhisattva precepts, which are called three pure precepts.
There are many ways of stating these precepts, but I like to use the ancient formula from earliest Buddhism: to avoid evil, to do good, and to benefit beings.
Three pure precepts.
Avoid evil.
Evil is of course an English word.
Unwholesomeness is the word more closely related to the Pali or Sanskrit word.
This precept means that we will practice a wise restraint.
It's the commitment to practice restraint in our lives.
It means to be calm and to recognize that our life is always being where we are when we are where we are.
That's our life.
We can't be, in other words, somewhere else when we're here.
And it can't be later when it's now.
So we just practice a wise restraint, being satisfied with what is in front of us.
We don't try to grab something extra for ourselves all the time.
We have some sense of a wise restraint.
We have precepts, rules to follow, common sense rules, and their purpose is to give us a life of enjoyment and contentment, so that we're not always reaching past where we are.
It's like when you practice walking meditation outdoors, which is something wonderful, a different way than we've been doing in the retreat.
Just by yourself, if you walk up and down, you look at what's in front of you, and if you see something beautiful, like a leaf or sunlight on the grass, you really appreciate that.
You don't look around all over the place.
You can see many things, but you don't do that.
You just look straight ahead, and whatever's ahead of you, you appreciate it.
Another time you can look all around, but in the practice of walking meditation you just look straight ahead.
It's like that.
A wise restraint: to just be with what's in front of us, not reaching for something extra.
The second precept, to do good.
This is the opposite of the first one.
It's the other side.
This one means that without stint, without holding back, we will practice all the positive virtues to benefit others.
All the positive practices of the Dharma: meditation practice, giving practice, loving kindness practice, energy, patience, wisdom, devotion, helping, studying, and so on.
Everything that's wholesome and positive we will do, just as we will restrain ourselves from doing that which is unwholesome, not positive.
So those are the first two of the three pure precepts.
And the third one is to benefit all beings.
The original statement of this precept from the oldest schools of Buddhism was not to benefit all beings but rather to purify the mind.
To avoid evil, do good and purify the mind.
But this was changed in Mahayana Buddhism to benefit all beings.
It's a very interesting teaching in itself, because in Mahayana Buddhism the understanding is that to purify the mind and to benefit all beings are exactly the same thing.
All beings are the mind.
And the mind is all beings.
That is the fundamental Mahayana understanding.
That's the mystery that we endeavor to appreciate through our sitting practice.
So when we say we benefit others, we don't understand others as others.
It means just to be aware, to be kind to ourselves and others equally.
Just to practice loving kindness with ourselves and others equally, because our self and another are not really different.
When we really understand finally who we are and we really understand finally who others are, then we know this.
So to benefit others, this is the spirit, the attitude with which we practice the first two pure precepts.
Wise restraint and doing good we practice with a spirit of benefiting others.
In other words, not uptight restraint, not uptight doing good, but free and easy, relaxed doing good.
Appreciating that self and other are one, and that following these precepts and not following these precepts are also one.
I said yesterday that the sixteen Bodhisattva precepts really come down to one precept: take refuge in Buddha.
And then that one precept we open up to three precepts: take refuge in Buddha, Dharma and Sangha.
And we want to explain what that means.
Take refuge in Buddha, Dharma and Sangha.
We say it means practice three pure precepts: to avoid evil, do good and benefit all beings.
That's what taking refuge in the triple treasure means.
And then how do we do good, avoid evil and benefit all beings?
What does that mean?
What does that look like?
The ten grave precepts are really the way of living and understanding the three pure precepts.
First, we don't kill anything.
We recognize the pure and holy ultimate nature of all of life, and we respect it in ourselves and all around us.
Second, we don't steal anything.
We practice, as a consequence of our activity in the Dharma, gratitude.
Gratitude arises in us and we make gratitude into a practice, recognizing that everything we have, down to the miracle of being a body and mind, everything that we have is a gift.
We never take anything unless we understand that it's a gift, unless we really know that it is given to us.
We don't misuse sexuality or sensuality.
We enjoy the pleasure of being embodied respectfully, without hurting anyone and without greed.
When pleasure comes in our lives, someone gives us lunch and it's good, we enjoy that and we're really grateful for it.
When there is no sexual pleasure or other sensual pleasure, then we enjoy its absence.
And we don't lie.
We speak the truth as far as we can, not indiscriminately but always with kindness, thoughtfully, not frivolously, and we recognize the awesome power of our words.
And we don't intoxicate ourselves or others.
This means we practice acceptance of our condition.
We don't try to change it.
If we're sick then we take medicine.
But even then, our spirit is to accept our condition.
If you're sick and you really want to get well, still, while you're sick, you are sick and you have to accept your being sick.
That's the way to get well.
If you're not sick, then, still, you accept your condition.
Practice is transformation.
Radical inner transformation.
And radical transformation starts with radical acceptance.
That is what it means not to intoxicate yourself.
Not to intoxicate others is a special precept for priests.
And all of us are priests of something, you know.
We're all priests of what we believe in and what we think is wonderful and important.
So this means don't try to intoxicate someone in beautiful and wonderful doctrine.
Whatever your doctrine may be that you believe in and you think is great, don't try to entice someone by getting them drunk with your doctrine.
Don't try to help them and show them the true way, which you understand and they don't.
Just love them and respond to them, but don't try to fix them and help them out with your profound understanding of how things are.
Don't intoxicate others.
And we don't slander others.
We don't dwell on others' faults, either in our minds or with our speech.
As Mel said in his talk in 1995, everyone including teachers has faults.
But also everyone including teachers has good points, too.
And we don't dwell on the faults.
We don't ignore them either.
But we don't decide that we're going to focus only on the faults.
That goes for one's self as well as others.
Also we don't praise self at the expense of others.
In other words, we don't raise ourselves up over others in our mind or in our speech.
Also we don't make ourselves lower than others in our mind or speech.
To lower ourselves is just another way of raising ourselves.
It seems strange, but it's really true.
It's like, oh, you think you're terrible and stupid and lazy?
That's nothing.
Look how terrible and stupid and lazy I am.
Much worse than you.
One-upmanship.
Down or up is the same upmanship.
And we're not possessive of anything.
Not even the Dharma.
We understand that it is not possible to possess anything.
Anyway, even our own body, even our own mind, certainly any material possessions that we may have or any brilliant thoughts or whatever we think we have, we don't really have that.
So naturally we practice generosity.
We don't harbor ill will.
When anger comes, we recognize it's anger.
We respect the power of anger.
We study the conditions that give rise to it.
We try to understand.
We try to transform anger or be patient with it.
But we don't indulge it.
We don't indulge in blaming.
We don't blame ourselves.
We don't blame others.
We just pay close attention to anger when it arises and we let it go.
And finally, we don't abuse the three treasures, which takes us back full circle to the beginning.
We respect the Buddha.
We unfold the Dharma through the story of our lives.
And we nourish the sangha by taking responsibility for it in whatever way that we can.
I'm so proud of myself.
Certainly much more could be said.
All I did here was recite and list these precepts.
But at least I did do that.
And many, many other depths will be found in your study and practice of the precepts.
I know that many of you have spent many discussion periods and study periods looking at these Bodhisattva precepts, and I know that you will continue to do that.
It's a lifetime's study.
It's inexhaustible.
And I'm sure that you will speak of them many times in the future and so will I with you.
But I did at least mention them.
So these 16 Bodhisattva precepts are zazen.
Zazen is every moment of our lives, which is a step, like I said last night, every moment of our lives is a step up, one step following on another, on and on and on.
More time to go in our retreat.
Please use the time well.
It's a fatal mistake to think, oh, I almost made it, only a few hours left.
Thinking this way is a guarantee for pain and suffering in the hours that remain.
Better to think that every moment is an endless retreat, and you'll face each moment with that spirit.
I want to apologize particularly to those of you who are new to the practice.
You have done a great job.
It is not too easy to sit here all this time.

You've done a great job, and I'm afraid that in speaking about these precepts and this and that that I've been talking about, I haven't really addressed the concerns that I know come up toward the beginning when you first take this up.
I know when I first began practicing and was hearing talks like this, my mind would be reeling, like, what are these people talking about?
And who cares?
I'm sitting here suffering.
Why don't they talk about that?
So I apologize for not talking about that at all.
But it's not because I haven't noticed.
It's just because somehow I was supposed to talk about the precepts.
I don't know.
It's just one of those things.
What a luxury it is to be able to practice together this way.
How fortunate we all are to have lives which give us enough food to eat and shelter that we can take days off in this way to do this.
Most of the people in this world that we live in could not dream of such a thing.
Couldn't even think of it.

If we're not sitting mindful of them and mindful of our many advantages, with a vow to remember this every day and somehow, whatever way we can find, give back for our gifts, then we've missed the boat.
We've misunderstood what we're doing.
So let's all please keep that in mind.
And now from now on, please everyone sit easily.
Okay?
Relax.
Let go.
Let your body melt into your cushion.
Have no concerns.
